detail:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes atrial fibrillation, often called AFib, as an irregular and often rapid heart rhythm that begins in the upper chambers of the heart. In AFib the atria beat chaotically instead of contracting in an organized pattern, so the lower chambers receive irregular signals and blood does not move through the heart as efficiently. CDC notes AFib can occur in brief episodes or become a lasting condition.

CDC notes that some people with AFib have no symptoms, while symptoms in others can include a fluttering or pounding heartbeat, fatigue, shortness of breath, weakness, and dizziness. Because blood can pool in the upper chambers, AFib is linked in the sources to blood clots and a higher risk of stroke, as well as heart failure. Clinicians diagnose AFib from the history and a physical exam together with tests that record the heart's electrical activity, such as an electrocardiogram.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about atrial fibrillation, symptoms, and stroke risk.
sourceName: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
summary: CDC describes atrial fibrillation as an irregular, often rapid rhythm in the heart's upper chambers that can cause no symptoms or a fluttering heartbeat and fatigue, and that raises the risk of stroke and heart failure.
takeaways: afib is an irregular rhythm in the heart's upper chambers
symptoms can include a fluttering heartbeat, fatigue, and breathlessness, and some people have none
sources link afib to blood clots, stroke, and heart failure
title: Atrial fibrillation: an irregular rhythm in the upper chambers
